item.title: Biosynthetic Gene Clusters of Astragalus Triterpenoid Saponins: From Genome Discovery to Synthetic Biology and Biomanufacturing Prospects.
item.abstract: Astragaloside IV is the best-characterized cycloartane-type triterpenoid saponin and the pharmacopoeial quality marker of Astragali Radix, with documented cardioprotective, antitumor, and immunomodulatory effects. Supply is constrained by long cultivation cycles that vary with production practice, replant disease, and phytochemical variability. Six representative genome assemblies are summarized for the genus, and they show that triterpenoid tailoring genes are partly, but not universally, clustered: a ~4 Mb biosynthetic gene cluster houses the oxidative and glycosylating enzymes, whereas the backbone synthase gene AmOSC3 lies outside it. The core route from 2,3-oxidosqualene to astragaloside IV has been reconstituted enzyme by enzyme; the in planta downstream routing, the acetylation steps forming astragalosides I and II, and the regulation, compartmentalization, transport, and storage of these saponins remain unresolved. Heterologous production is at the proof-of-concept stage: 1.04 mg/L cycloastragenol in yeast (versus the 25 g/L artemisinic acid precedent), 2.224 mg astragaloside IV/g dry weight in Nicotiana benthamiana, and a 4.2-fold total-astragaloside increase in AmUGT15-overexpressing hairy roots. This review consolidates genome mining, pathway biochemistry, and synthetic-biology engineering; benchmarks current platforms against pharmacopoeial quality requirements; and maps the bottlenecks between proof of concept and sustainable biomanufacturing.

item.title: Tuned Fitness Landscapes for Benchmarking Model-Guided Protein Design.
item.abstract: Machine learning-guided directed evolution (MLDE) is an emerging paradigm of protein design where ML models trained on experimental data are used to guide exploration of a protein fitness landscape. Building an MLDE pipeline involves many design choices across the design-build-test-learn loop ranging from data collection strategies to modeling. The cost of collecting experimental data makes benchmarking every component of these pipelines prohibitively difficult, necessitating the development of synthetic landscapes. In this work, we develop a framework called SLIP ("Synthetic Landscape Inference for Proteins") for constructing synthetic landscapes with tunable difficulty based on Potts models. This framework can be extended to any protein family for which there is a sequence alignment. We show that our tuning framework provides landscapes sufficiently challenging to benchmark MLDE pipelines. SLIP is open-source and is available at https://github.com/google-research/slip.

item.title: Metadata-Driven Project-Level Analysis and Noise Modeling for Amplicon Sequencing Data Using CRISPResso2.
item.abstract: Here we present a lightweight workflow designed to improve the robustness and scalability of high-throughput amplicon sequencing analysis while leveraging CRISPResso2. To handle large batch processing without sensitive runtime interruptions, our pipeline processes samples sequentially, allowing the analysis to resume from the last successfully completed sample if an error occurs. The workflow implements a fallback mechanism for failed runs, automated extraction and separate processing of control samples, and a background noise model derived from control libraries within defined editing windows. Validation using spike-in datasets across Cas9, base editing, and prime editing demonstrated that our noise-adjusted estimates deviated from the ground truth by only 0.1-0.6%, whereas native CRISPResso2 caused a 1.5-3.7% overestimation. Unlike existing tools such as CRISPECTOR, which focus primarily on CRISPR-Cas9, our approach supports multiple editing modalities and enables project-level organization of large datasets. Input complexity is reduced through configurable flags and modular metadata tables, minimizing manual parameter entry. Together, these features provide a flexible, fault-tolerant, and highly accurate framework for analyzing large genome editing datasets.

item.title: How to train your microbe: editing environmental bacteria.
item.abstract: Genome editing is an essential tool in microbiology, enabling researchers to assess gene function, link genotype to phenotype, and design microbes with specific features. Most tools have been developed in model bacteria, and adapting them to environmental species remains time- and resource-intensive. This review provides a framework for engineering environmental bacteria, including assessment of genetic tractability, considerations for overcoming challenges in recalcitrant systems, and an overview of techniques with guidance on tool selection. We discuss the emerging field of microbiome editing, where genome modifications can be delivered to bacteria within complex microbial communities and hosts, opening new possibilities for mechanistic studies across diverse environments. These advances promise to shift functional microbiology from reductionist, isolate-based approaches toward contextually informed, mechanistic investigations.

item.title: Programmable RNA therapeutics: converging vaccination and on-demand disease treatment via self-adaptive RNA platforms.
item.abstract: RNA technology, most prominently messenger RNA (mRNA), has transformed vaccine development by enabling rapid, sequence-specific antigen design, scalable manufacturing, and transient protein expression. Its long-term significance, however, extends beyond prophylactic vaccination. This Perspective argues that mRNA should be conceptualised as a programmable therapeutic platform capable of integrating vaccination, immune modulation, and on-demand disease treatment. Current mRNA vaccines deliver predefined antigenic instructions, whereas emerging RNA systems, including self-amplifying RNA (saRNA), circular RNA, sequence-engineered mRNA, and targeted lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), may support more adaptable therapeutic functions. Such platforms could prime immunity, replace deficient proteins, encode antibodies, reprogramme immune cells, or induce antigen-specific tolerance. The concept of self-adaptive RNA-based therapeutics remains at an early stage and should not be overstated; most existing systems are programmable at the design stage rather than biologically autonomous after administration. Nonetheless, this conceptual position is no longer purely speculative: the first regulatory approval of a self-amplifying RNA vaccine and controlled-trial evidence of clinical benefit from a personalised neoantigen mRNA therapeutic in resected melanoma indicate that programmable RNA platforms are beginning to move from concept to clinical validation across both the prophylactic and therapeutic ends of the spectrum. Key challenges include tissue-specific delivery, expression control, innate immune activation, repeat dosing, safety assessment, regulatory classification, and equitable access. A self-adaptive RNA-based framework does not replace existing vaccines or biologics but extends them towards responsive, personalised, and temporally controlled therapy.

item.title: An oral delivery platform for protein drugs: PDA/PEGylated engineered probiotics responsively release TLR5 agonists to prevent radiation enteritis.
item.abstract: Oral protein delivery is hindered by gastrointestinal degradation and poor mucosal bioavailability. Engineered probiotics offer a promising strategy for oral protein delivery, but their therapeutic efficacy is often limited by insufficient payload expression and low secretion efficiency. Here, we present a living oral platform that integrates high-yield protein biosynthesis with on-demand intestinal release. By gene manipulation and FLAG tagging, we dramatically upregulate constitutive expression of GP532 in probiotic Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN), while installing an arabinose-inducible autolytic switch for efficient intracellular payload release. A dual-layer coating of polydopamine (PDA) and polyethylene glycol (PEG) confers acid resistance and mucus penetration, while allowing arabinose to permeate and blocking digestive enzymes. Upon single oral gavage in a murine model of radiation enteritis, our formulation achieves therapeutic efficacy fully equivalent to systemic injection of GP532 in mitigating intestinal injury. Critically, unlike injectable biologics, this living platform promotes the restoration of gut microbial community structure and beneficial taxa, a unique benefit unattainable by parenteral administration, while the engineered strain is completely cleared within 24 h. By synergizing genetic circuit engineering, surface chemical modification, and in situ luminal release, this work establishes a single-dose, orally effective alternative to injectable protein therapy, offering a transformative strategy for the prevention of radiation enteritis with the added benefit of microbiome maintenance.

item.title: Genome Editing for Earliness and Plant Architecture in Cucurbit Crops: Recent Advances and Future Perspectives.
item.abstract: Earliness and plant architecture are major breeding targets in cucurbit crops because they influence crop duration, early yield, planting density, canopy management, and production efficiency. This review summarizes genetic, molecular, and genome-editing advances related to flowering, sex expression, fruit development, stem elongation, branching, and canopy architecture in cucumber, melon, watermelon, Cucurbita species, and other cucurbits. Current evidence shows that earlier flowering or increased femaleness does not necessarily lead to earlier commercial maturity, while compact growth must be evaluated together with yield, fruit quality, and environmental adaptation. CRISPR/Cas9 knockout remains the most established editing approach, whereas base editing, cis-regulatory editing, multiplex editing, developmental-regulator-assisted regeneration, and DNA-free RNP delivery offer promising routes toward more precise trait optimization. Major constraints include genotype-dependent transformation, pleiotropic effects, limited validation in elite germplasm, and scarce direct evidence for shortening fruit-development duration. An evidence-guided framework is proposed that links trait definition, functional genomics, target prioritization, tailored genome editing, whole-plant evaluation, and breeding deployment. Future progress will depend on quantitatively tuned alleles and coordinated optimization of reproductive timing, canopy architecture, productivity, fruit quality, and environmental stability.

item.title: Emerging Computational Advances in Simulating PCSK9 Variant Dynamics for Therapeutic Design Against Hypercholesterolemia.
item.abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a premier model for precision medicine, having moved from genetic discovery to approved therapeutics within two decades. Yet despite the clinical success of monoclonal antibodies, small interfering RNA and the newly approved oral macrocyclic-peptide inhibitor class, targeting PCSK9 remains a demanding biophysical challenge. Clinical translation has concentrated almost entirely on the rigid, well-resolved subtilisin-like catalytic domain that interfaces with the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). By contrast, the C-terminal cysteine- and histidine-rich domain (CHRD), which governs allosteric regulation, protein trafficking and post-translational modification, is highly disordered and largely elusive in experimental structures, leaving a critical regulatory network therapeutically unexploited. This review examines how advanced computational biology is bridging that structural gap, organizing the computational landscape of PCSK9 around the biophysical mechanisms of gain- and loss-of-function variants. We detail how explicit-solvent molecular dynamics, free-energy calculations and cryptic-pocket detection expose the functional plasticity and allosteric networks that static crystallography cannot capture, and we evaluate the convergence of these physics-based approaches with artificial intelligence, including deep-learning structure prediction and generative design of de novo nanobody and peptide binders. Therapeutic development and the structural literature currently point in diverging directions: drug discovery remains focused on the crowded LDLR-binding interface, whereas computational methods are beginning to identify candidate sites beyond it. We argue that the next advance in PCSK9 therapeutics will come from integrating generative artificial intelligence with rigorous enhanced sampling in a unified pipeline, deliberately shifting focus toward the disordered regulatory domains that have evaded classical screening.

item.title: Not All EVs Are Equal: Functional Heterogeneity of Extracellular Vesicles in Neuroregenerative Therapies.
item.abstract: Extracellular vesicles (EVs) are increasingly being investigated as cell-free therapies for neurological diseases. However, their clinical application remains limited by biological and functional heterogeneity. EVs should therefore not be considered as a single, uniform therapeutic product defined only by their cell of origin, size, or conventional vesicle classification. EV composition and activity are influenced by extrinsic factors, including donor and tissue source, culture conditions, and isolation procedures, as well as by intrinsic mechanisms of vesicle biogenesis and selective cargo loading. Some vesicles may have beneficial therapeutic effects, whereas others may show little biological activity or act on unintended cellular targets. For this reason, EVs may be better classified according to biological function rather than only physical properties or cellular origin. A functionality-based classification could improve potency assessment, dose selection, reproducibility, and the development of consistent EV-based products. EV properties can be modulated by selecting appropriate parental cells, modifying culture conditions, or using genetic or metabolic engineering to alter EV production and cargo. Single-vesicle approaches can reveal differences between EV subpopulations and identify those responsible for specific biological effects. Overall, understanding EV heterogeneity may provide a rational basis for developing reproducible and disease-specific EV therapies for neurological and neurodegenerative disorders.

item.title: Mesenchymal Stem/Stromal Cell-Derived Extracellular Vesicles for Immunomodulation in Osteoarthritis.
item.abstract: Osteoarthritis (OA) is a heterogeneous disorder affecting multiple joint tissues, in which structural degeneration may be accompanied by varying degrees of synovial inflammation and immune-stromal dysregulation. Mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs) have demonstrated immunomodulatory and tissue-protective properties, increasingly linked to paracrine signaling. Comparative studies suggest that extracellular vesicles (EVs) make an important, but not exclusive, contribution to MSC paracrine activity, with soluble secretome components providing potentially complementary effects. Drawing on literature identified primarily through PubMed and Scopus and clinical trial records from ClinicalTrials.gov (updated through September 2026), this narrative review examines the immunomodulatory role of MSC-derived EVs (MSC-EVs) in OA, with emphasis on their interactions with the joint immune microenvironment and their contribution to tissue protection. Across experimental OA models, MSC-EVs have been reported to reduce synovitis, cartilage degeneration, subchondral bone alterations, and pain-related outcomes, although responses vary with MSC source, EV composition, engineering strategies, disease context, and treatment regimen. Mechanistically, the most consistent evidence supports modulation of macrophage-associated inflammatory responses, whereas effects on adaptive immune populations remain less established and are largely derived from non-OA models. Clinical evidence remains limited and currently provides mainly preliminary information on feasibility and short-term tolerability, with insufficient evidence to establish therapeutic efficacy. Overall, MSC-EVs represent a potential cell-free immunomodulatory approach for OA, but standardized manufacturing, product characterization, dosing, and rigorously controlled clinical trials are required to define their therapeutic value.

item.title: Circulating tumor DNA in Hodgkin lymphoma: biological classification, molecular residual disease, and integration with PET response.
item.abstract: Circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA) and its tumor-derived fraction, circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA), enable non-invasive tumor genotyping, longitudinal disease monitoring, and molecular residual disease (MRD) assessment. Classical Hodgkin lymphoma (cHL) is particularly suitable for ctDNA-based analysis because malignant Hodgkin and Reed-Sternberg cells usually constitute only a small fraction of the tumor mass, whereas plasma may contain a strong tumor-derived DNA signal. This narrative review summarizes the potential applications of cfDNA-based ctDNA analysis in hematologic malignancies, with a focused emphasis on cHL. We discuss pre-analytical and analytical requirements, including plasma processing, tumor-informed and tumor-naive sequencing, error suppression, droplet digital PCR, and control for clonal hematopoiesis. We then synthesize evidence for ctDNA as a dual-readout biomarker: a baseline tool for non-invasive biological classification and a dynamic measure of molecular response. Published studies identify cHL genomic subtypes, associations with the tumor microenvironment, and prognostic information complementary to PET and conventional risk factors. Age-specific evidence is uneven, and most studies demonstrate analytical feasibility or prognosis rather than benefit from a ctDNA-triggered intervention. ctDNA-MRD should complement FDG-PET/CT; it cannot localize disease or currently replace established staging and response criteria. Routine implementation will require harmonized sample handling, validated assays and reporting thresholds, external quality assessment, and prospective trials demonstrating that ctDNA-guided treatment improves disease control, toxicity, or quality of life.

item.title: Translocation of the environmental bacterium Aquitalea magnusonii promotes systemic inflammation and liver fibrosis in chronic liver disease.
item.abstract:
BACKGROUND & AIMS: Impaired mucosal barrier integrity facilitates translocation of the gut microbiome into the circulation and the liver, thereby exacerbating the severity of chronic liver diseases (CLD). This study aimed to investigate the pathogenic role of non-commensal environmental bacteria, specifically Aquitalea magnusonii in CLD progression by assessing its ability to cross the intestinal barrier and induce systemic inflammation and liver fibrosis.
METHODS: Using an integrated translational framework, patient blood analyses were combined with multi-omics profiling, human intestinal epithelial models, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC), hepatic stellate cells (HSC), monocytes, and alcoholic (ALD) and metabolic dysfunction-associated (MASLD) models to evaluate the translocation, virulence, inflammatory and fibrotic potential of A. magnusonii in CLD.
RESULTS: Non-commensal environmental bacteria, including Aquitalea spp. were detected in multiple organs in both ALD and MASLD models. Detection of Aquitalea DNA in patient samples and other non-commensal environmental bacteria in tap water suggested potential aquatic reservoirs. A. magnusonii produced 12 acute-on-chronic liver failure (ACLF) associated metabolites and its outer membrane vesicles (OMV) were enriched in virulence-related proteins, supporting roles in adhesion, invasion, and immune activation. In addition, gavage with A. magnusonii led to a substantial dysbiotic shift in the gut microbiome. Mechanistically, the cell-free supernatant of A. magnusonii culture activated TLR2- and TLR4-dependent pro-inflammatory signaling pathways. Exposure to A. magnusonii or its pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) significantly increased inflammation and fibrosis in vitro and in vivo.
CONCLUSION: Non-commensal environmental bacteria, in the example of A. magnusonii, can translocate across the intestinal barrier and promote liver inflammation and fibrogenesis via metabolite production, virulence-associated OMV, and innate immune activation.
IMPACT AND IMPLICATIONS: This study highlights an underrecognized role of non-commensal environmental bacteria in chronic liver disease. Beyond gut commensals, detection of non-commensal environmental microbes such as Aquitalea was associated with markers of more advanced liver disease, while experimental studies of A. magnusonii support biological plausibility for a potential contributory role. These findings highlight the importance of considering environmental reservoirs and non-commensal pathogens in microbial contributions to CLD pathogenesis.

item.title: Microbial Biotransformation of Plant Bioactive Compounds: Mechanisms, Enhanced Bioactivities, and Applications in Functional Food Development.
item.abstract: Plant-derived bioactive compounds, including polyphenols, flavonoids, alkaloids, terpenoids, and saponins, possess diverse health-promoting properties but are often limited by poor bioaccessibility, structural complexity, and low stability. Microbial biotransformation provides a green and food-compatible strategy for modifying these compounds through enzymatic reactions and metabolic processes, generating derivatives with improved accessibility and potential functional properties. This review summarizes recent advances in microbial transformation mediated by lactic acid bacteria, Bacillus, yeasts, and filamentous fungi, focusing on key transformation pathways, including deglycosylation, hydrolysis, oxidation-reduction, methylation, and glycosylation, as well as their enzymatic mechanisms. The applications of transformed products in fermented foods, functional ingredients, and nutraceuticals are discussed, along with their potential antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, metabolic regulatory, and bioavailability-related effects. Current challenges, including incomplete mechanistic understanding, process standardization, safety evaluation, scale-up, and regulatory issues, are highlighted. Future integration of multi-omics, synthetic biology, enzyme engineering, and intelligent fermentation technologies will enhance the efficiency and industrial potential of microbial transformation systems for developing safe and evidence-based functional food ingredients.

item.title: Preparation of a soluble 1,3-β-glucan from baker's yeast by water-only autoclave treatment and evaluation of its Dectin-1 antagonist activity.
item.abstract: Soluble β-glucans have attracted considerable attention as modulators of Dectin-1 signaling and are expected to have applications as immunomodulatory agents. However, the preparation of biologically active soluble β-glucans from baker's yeast generally requires multiple chemical extraction and purification steps. Herein, we developed a simple, chemical-free method for preparing a soluble β-glucan fraction from baker's yeast by prolonged autoclave treatment in water at 135 °C. The resulting fraction, designated autoclave-treated β-glucan (AT-BG), was characterized by gel filtration chromatography, Smith degradation, and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, and its Dectin-1 antagonist activity was evaluated using a human Dectin-1-expressing THP-1 cell-based assay and a cell-free receptor-binding assay. AT-BG inhibited Dectin-1-dependent TNF-α production in a concentration-dependent manner and exhibited greater antagonistic activity than laminarin without detectable cytotoxicity. Fractionation analysis demonstrated that the antagonist activity was predominantly associated with the >10 kDa fraction. Although this apparent molecular weight exceeded that expected for soluble Dectin-1 antagonists, Smith degradation markedly reduced the apparent molecular size. These findings suggest that the relatively large apparent molecular weight of native AT-BG is primarily attributable to periodate-sensitive side-chain structures rather than to the functional β-glucan backbone. In a cell-free competition assay, AT-BG inhibited Dectin-1 binding to immobilized β-glucan more effectively than laminarin, and Smith-degraded AT-BG retained this activity, which places the binding on the periodate-resistant glucan backbone. Collectively, these results establish a simple, water-only strategy for preparing a biologically active soluble Dectin-1 antagonist from baker's yeast.
